title: Does the 2023 law protect election commissioners?
claim: The 2023 law gives election commissioners protection against legal proceedings for official-duty acts.
summary: Section 16 provides a substantial protection, with an official-duty connection in its wording.
context: Gandhi criticised the protection during the December 2025 electoral-reforms debate. This checks the existence of that provision, not the legality of his proposed retrospective response.
evidence: Section 16 bars courts from entertaining or continuing civil or criminal proceedings against current or former CECs and ECs for acts, things or words while acting, or purporting to act, in official duty or function. The parliamentary bill text inspected here and Indian Express’s quotation of the enacted section agree. The wording contains no express good-faith qualifier.
finding: Supported for the existence of official-duty protection. Describing it as unlimited immunity for everything a commissioner does would exceed the text.
limit: This does not establish misconduct, rule out every form of judicial review, or determine how a court would apply the provision to particular facts. The enacted India Code PDF was not retrievable; no later court outcome is certified.
sources: Rajya Sabha, bill as passed, section 16, PDF page 5
Indian Express, speech attribution and enacted section 16, 10 December 2025

before_2014: The pre-2014 institutional baseline was the 1991 Election Commission law, later amended to regulate a multi-member commission. Its subject matter was service conditions and the transaction of business. It was in force during UPA as well as the preceding NDA period.

The 2023 legislation replaced that law and included the express protection discussed here. This review has not reconstructed every pre-2014 statutory defence, procedural sanction or judicial immunity potentially available to commissioners. Absence of an identical provision in one statute would not establish absence of all legal protection.
history.comparison: The valid comparison is the specific statutory wording and scope. Claims that commissioners previously had no protection, or that Congress could lawfully prosecute every official decision, require further legal analysis.
sources: 1991 Election Commission Act, reproduced legal text
PRS, appointment arrangements before the March 2023 interim judgment

title: A bullock-race crowd labelled a Bihar rally
claim: A huge crowd video shows a Rahul Gandhi rally in Bihar.
summary: The identified earlier upload concerns a bullock-cart event in Maharashtra.
context: A crowd clip was presented as evidence of attendance at Gandhi’s Bihar mobilisation in August 2025.
evidence: AFP found a 28 June 2025 Instagram upload identifying a bullock-cart event at Pedgaon in Maharashtra. It compared venue features with mapping imagery. That earlier source contradicts the Bihar-rally caption.
finding: False for this video’s claimed event and location. It is not evidence of the attendance at the alleged Gandhi rally.
limit: The earlier upload date does not independently certify the exact day the race took place. This check does not estimate attendance at either event, and full original playback was not repeated here.

history.scope: Historical context: establish the original event before making a political comparison.
before_2014: The original upload appeared before the August 2025 political caption and identified a different kind of gathering in a different state. No pre-2014 Congress rally provides a valid attendance baseline for identifying this particular scene. Historical crowd comparisons would require separately authenticated dates, venues and counting methods. None of those can turn this Maharashtra footage into a Bihar event.
history.comparison: The useful history is the clip’s publication sequence. It debunks the attribution while leaving the size of any genuine Bihar rally to separate evidence.

review_note: Reviewed 18 October 2026 (IST). Initial publication. Historical context included.

title: The man in the selfie was a lawyer, not the judge
claim: A photograph shows the judge who granted Gandhi bail taking a selfie with him.
summary: AFP identified the man as lawyer Syed Mahmood Hasan, not magistrate Alok Verma.
context: The image circulated around Gandhi’s July 2025 court appearance with an allegation about the judicial officer.
evidence: AFP compared official photographs, checked the lawyer’s professional identity and interviewed Hasan. Its investigation identifies the person beside Gandhi as the lawyer and distinguishes him from the named magistrate.
finding: False for the identity claim attached to this photograph. The image does not substantiate the alleged selfie with the judge.
limit: This finding concerns identification in the photograph. It does not assess the merits or eventual outcome of the underlying case, and it does not establish every interaction Gandhi may have had.

history.scope: Historical context: establish the original event before making a political comparison.
before_2014: The July 2025 caption tied a photograph to a particular court proceeding, so the relevant historical record consists of the image’s provenance and the identities of those present. Congress’s pre-2014 legal or judicial record cannot establish who appears in this later photograph. Allegations about a specific officer require evidence identifying that officer, rather than a general argument about political influence.
history.comparison: The documented identity comparison answers the photo claim. A broader historical argument about courts would need independent records and cannot substitute for that identification.

review_note: Reviewed 18 October 2026 (IST). Initial publication. Historical context included.

title: What followed the Rath Yatra “drama” remark?
claim: Gandhi called the Jagannath Rath Yatra itself a drama in a July 2025 speech.
summary: The clipped video omits his explanation: he was alleging preferential treatment for the Adani family.
context: AFP traced the excerpt to a longer News18 Odia recording of Gandhi’s 11 July 2025 Bhubaneswar rally.
evidence: The excerpt appears around 32 seconds in that recording. AFP’s comparison restores the following words, in which Gandhi alleges that chariots were stopped for Adani and his family. That continuation explains what he was describing as drama.
finding: Misleading when the excerpt is presented as an unqualified description of the religious festival. The omitted allegation is necessary context for interpreting his remark.
limit: This relies on AFP’s published comparison; full original playback was not independently completed. It does not independently establish a deliberate delay, VIP favouritism, the truth of his allegation, or his personal religious intentions.

history.scope: Event-specific; no valid government-era performance comparison
before_2014: The source event is the July 2025 rally and the alleged treatment of visitors at that year’s Rath Yatra. No pre-2014 comparison of chariot stoppages, VIP access or Congress policy was established from the reviewed sources. A historical incident would require its own date, venue and evidence.
history.comparison: The immediate question is what Gandhi called drama in this recording. Neither a favourable nor an unfavourable account of a previous government changes the omitted continuation. His separate allegation about the 2025 event remains unverified.

title: Two altered photographs used to imply a meeting
claim: Two photographs show Gandhi posing with YouTuber Jyoti Malhotra, arrested in an espionage case.
summary: AFP traced both scenes to earlier photographs with other people and found face replacements.
context: The images circulated after Malhotra’s arrest in May 2025. Arrest allegations are not treated here as a finding of guilt.
evidence: AFP identified one original photograph posted by Aditi Singh on 16 December 2017 and another posted by Gandhi on 18 September 2022 showing a different person. The circulating versions replace the women’s faces with Malhotra’s.
finding: False for these two photographs as evidence of the alleged meetings. The originals contradict their claimed identification.
limit: This does not establish whether Gandhi and Malhotra ever met on another occasion, or determine her case’s outcome. The review relies on AFP’s published source-image comparison.

history.scope: Historical context: establish the original event before making a political comparison.
before_2014: The source photographs date to 2017 and 2022, both after the pre-2014 period the site examines for policy comparisons. Their earlier publication matters because it reveals who appeared before the face replacements. Congress-era security policy cannot authenticate these altered portraits. Even an authentic photograph would need separate evidence before it could support an allegation of knowledge of, or involvement in, another person’s alleged activities.
history.comparison: The chronology supports an image-manipulation finding, with no conclusion about criminal guilt or every possible prior association.

review_note: Reviewed 18 October 2026 (IST). Initial publication. Historical context included.

title: Article 15(5): an existing power, not an automatic quota
claim: Article 15(5) already provides a constitutional basis for reservation in private educational institutions.
summary: The enabling provision exists. It has exceptions and requires legislation.
context: Congress’s account of Gandhi’s 30 April 2025 briefing, published on 22 May, records him citing Article 15(5) and asking for implementation. This check concerns the existence and scope of the provision.
evidence: The official Gazette’s 93rd Amendment text inserts Article 15(5). It permits special admission provisions made by law for socially and educationally backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, including in private aided or unaided institutions. It excludes minority institutions protected by Article 30(1). The constitutional power is enabling, rather than an automatic uniform quota.
finding: Supported on the narrow claim that the constitutional power already exists. The provision does not itself impose one uniform quota in every private institution. The implementing law and the institution’s status matter.
limit: This does not establish which institutions were complying in April 2025, what further legislation was required in each jurisdiction, or whether a particular proposed quota would survive legal challenge.
sources: Congress, account of 30 April 2025 briefing, published 22 May

before_2014: This enabling power dates to UPA-I. The 93rd Amendment, assented to on 20 January 2006, inserted Article 15(5), covering special admission provisions made by law, including for private aided and unaided institutions, with the stated minority-institution exception.

UPA also enacted the Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006, notified in January 2007. Its defined central-institution scope must not be confused with all private colleges. Section 3 sets SC, ST and OBC percentages, subject to exclusions and implementation provisions.
history.comparison: Gandhi is invoking an existing constitutional power established under Congress-led government. Whether Congress or later governments fully used that power in each category of private institution is a separate implementation question.
sources: India Code, Central Educational Institutions Act, 2006, sections 3–6

corrections.note: Replaced an incorrect PIB link, which concerned minority-education legislation, with the official 93rd Amendment Gazette. Rewrote the evidence paragraph to cite the text actually inspected. Supported verdict unchanged.

title: China and the 4,000 sq km claim
claim: Rahul Gandhi said China was occupying 4,000 square kilometres of Indian territory.
summary: The statement is documented. The precise area is not independently established by the sources reviewed.
context: Congress published his 3 April 2025 Lok Sabha intervention. It repeats the 4,000 sq km figure. A party transcript establishes what Congress says he said, not whether the territorial measurement is correct.
evidence: In February 2025, the Defence Ministry rejected his attribution of territorial remarks to the Army Chief. It distinguished disrupted patrolling from the words Gandhi attributed to the chief. This is the government’s response, not an independent boundary survey.
finding: Keep two questions separate: whether the Army Chief made the attributed statement, and whether China occupies the claimed area. These sources do not independently verify the precise 4,000 sq km figure. A government denial alone does not disprove it.
limit: No independent geospatial calculation or agreed baseline was obtained. This assessment concerns the April 2025 claim, not a current map of territorial control.

history.scope: Earlier official position; no matched territorial measurement
before_2014: The territorial dispute predates 2014. MEA’s 2013 official compilation, during UPA-II, records approximately 38,000 sq km of Indian territory under Chinese occupation in the then state of Jammu and Kashmir. That figure is a long-standing territorial position, not an estimate of changes after 2020. The indexed extract was retrieved; the full compilation was blocked.

There was also a pre-2014 border-management framework: the 1993 peace-and-tranquility agreement under P. V. Narasimha Rao’s Congress government, the 1996 confidence-building agreement under the United Front, and UPA-era agreements or protocols in 2005, 2012 and 2013. These sought to manage the disputed border; signing them was not a final territorial settlement.

Consequently, neither “all occupied territory was lost after 2014” nor subtraction of Gandhi’s 4,000 from the old 38,000 is a sound inference. One must identify the polygons, baseline date and whether a number concerns territorial control, access to patrol points or buffer arrangements.
history.comparison: The historical record rules out treating Chinese occupation as a new post-2014 phenomenon. It neither confirms nor disproves a distinct recent 4,000 sq km change. A same-area, same-definition geospatial comparison is still missing.
sources: MEA, India’s Foreign Relations 2013, printed page 1038, indexed extract; full PDF retrieval blocked
MEA, 2013 Border Defence Cooperation agreement and earlier treaty chronology
Prime Minister’s Office, former Prime Ministers and tenure dates

title: Maharashtra’s voter growth: dates before conclusions
claim: Maharashtra added about 39 lakh voters in five months in 2024, compared with about 32 lakh in the preceding five years.
summary: Contemporaneous reports support the attribution and a roughly 39-lakh short-period increase. The complete two-period comparison was not reproduced.
context: NDTV reported this comparison at Gandhi’s 7 February 2025 press conference. This is distinct from his earlier, larger numerical claim in Parliament.
evidence: A December 2024 Times of India report says the Election Commission put additions since the Lok Sabha election at 39 lakh. That supports the broad short-period magnitude, but does not reproduce both of Gandhi’s periods from original dated rolls. Additions, deletions and net growth must be distinguished.
finding: Unverified for the complete comparison in this review. The shorter-period figure has reported official corroboration; that is not equivalent to auditing the underlying rolls. An increase alone does not prove fraudulent registrations or a changed election result.
limit: Needed: original electorate totals at consistent cut-off dates for all three endpoints, including the treatment of service voters, additions and deletions. No voter-level audit was completed. The separate adult-population comparison is outside this verdict.
sources: Times of India, reported ECI response, 4 December 2024

before_2014: Pre-2014 election records exist in the ECI’s historical statistical archive. Maharashtra’s earlier Assembly elections provide a potential benchmark, but an Assembly electorate total, a Lok Sabha total and a revision-date roll need not have identical cut-offs or categories.

This review has not extracted an audited pre-2014 series of additions and deletions for a matching five-month window. Calling an older five-year change the Congress-era “normal rate” without age-cohort, registration-drive and cut-off adjustments would produce a weak comparison. Union and state governments also must not be treated as the electoral registration authority.
history.comparison: The missing older benchmark is explicit. Historical averages alone cannot establish whether particular 2024 entries were eligible or whether an election result was affected. The original two-period claim remains unverified.

title: Manufacturing: which share, which year?
claim: Manufacturing fell from 15.3% of GDP in 2014 to 12.6%, its lowest share in 60 years.
summary: The statement is documented. The exact comparison and the 60-year low were not reproduced from a consistent statistical series.
context: Congress’s published extracts attribute these figures to Gandhi’s 3 February 2025 Lok Sabha speech. This is a party account of his statement, not independent validation of the statistics.
evidence: The Finance Ministry’s July 2024 Economic Survey summary reports a manufacturing GVA share of 14.3% for FY2022–23. That is not automatically a comparable measure: GDP and total GVA are different denominators, and current-price and constant-price shares differ. A share can decline even while the level of manufacturing output grows.
finding: Unverified for the exact endpoints and historical minimum. The reviewed official summary alone neither reproduces nor disproves his comparison. A different year or denominator must not be presented as a direct rebuttal.
limit: Needed: the original series, its vintage, price basis, reference years and a comparable six-decade history. No complete historical series was reconstructed. This is not a verdict on the overall success of Make in India.
sources: Congress, extracts of 3 February speech, published 20 February 2025
Finance Ministry, Economic Survey summary, 22 July 2024

before_2014: Manufacturing’s relatively small share was already a policy concern under UPA. In October 2011 its Cabinet approved a National Manufacturing Policy targeting at least a 25% GDP share and 100 million additional jobs by 2022. Those were future goals, not achieved 2011 levels.

This predates Make in India and shows continuity in the ambition to expand manufacturing. It does not by itself provide the consistent observed GDP series required to test Gandhi’s 2014 endpoint or his six-decade minimum. A policy target cannot substitute for the statistical baseline.
history.comparison: Compare actual shares using one source vintage, denominator and price basis. Credit for announcing a manufacturing goal and responsibility for outcomes are different questions. The exact numerical claim is unchanged by this policy history.

title: The CJI and the election-commissioner selection panel
claim: The Chief Justice of India was excluded from the selection committee under the new election-commissioner appointment law.
summary: The 2023 law uses a Cabinet minister in place of the CJI in the court’s interim arrangement.
context: Congress’s extracts of Gandhi’s 3 February 2025 speech record his objection to the CJI’s exclusion. This checks the committee’s composition, not his allegation of a calculated political strategy.
evidence: Section 7 names the Prime Minister, the Lok Sabha opposition leader and a Union Cabinet minister nominated by the Prime Minister. The reviewed parliamentary text is the bill passed by Rajya Sabha on 12 December 2023; Indian Express’s account of the enacted law corroborates that composition. The Supreme Court’s earlier arrangement included the CJI pending legislation.
finding: Supported for the change in membership. The court’s arrangement was interim, not a permanent statutory entitlement subsequently taken away. Appointment remains formally by the President on the committee’s recommendation.
limit: This historical check does not establish bias in an individual appointment or certify the outcome of subsequent constitutional litigation. The enacted India Code PDF could not be retrieved in this review.
sources: Rajya Sabha, bill as passed, section 7, PDF page 2

before_2014: Before 2014, including under the Congress-led UPA governments of 2004–14, election commissioners were appointed by the President through the executive process. The 1991 service-conditions law did not create a selection panel containing either the opposition leader or the Chief Justice of India.

The CJI panel came from the Supreme Court’s March 2023 interim direction, pending parliamentary legislation. It was not the appointment system inherited from Congress. The December 2023 law then specified a different panel with an opposition member and two executive members.
history.comparison: The CJI’s exclusion is supported against the March 2023 arrangement. It would be historically inaccurate to describe it as the removal of a long-standing Congress-era CJI role. The old executive system also does not settle whether the new panel is sufficiently independent.
sources: PRS, appointment arrangements before the March 2023 interim judgment

title: UPA’s caste-survey record: launched, but not published in full
claim: UPA initiated a caste-enumeration exercise in 2011 but did not deliver the published caste breakdown now being demanded.
summary: The separate SECC exercise was launched. The caste output and the main population census must be distinguished.
context: Ranchi reporting of Gandhi’s 18 November 2024 briefing records his acknowledgment of a UPA implementation mistake. This check assesses the historical core, not whether that mistake alone explains every later delay.
evidence: The Cabinet decided in September 2010 to enumerate caste separately from the main 2011 census. The 2011 Rural Development review records the SECC launch in Tripura. A July 2022 Home Ministry reply says SECC’s non-caste data were published while caste data were not.
finding: Supported with this distinction: saying UPA never collected caste information would be wrong. Launch, field collection, classification, publication and policy use are different stages.
limit: The evidence does not apportion responsibility for every delay across UPA and later governments, validate all collected returns, or certify a current national caste dataset.
sources: Times of India, Ranchi briefing reported 19 November 2024
Rural Development Ministry, SECC launch and progress, 2011 review

before_2014: The UPA Cabinet’s 2010 statement itself noted that the last detailed all-caste census tabulation and publication was in 1931. Post-independence population censuses did continue SC and ST enumeration. “No caste data since independence” is therefore too sweeping.

SECC was a separate exercise, not an interchangeable name for the main Census 2011. Its existence shows the demand did not begin in 2024, while its unpublished caste component shows that announcing an exercise did not complete the requested public statistical record.
history.comparison: Both UPA’s uncompleted publication and the continued non-publication recorded by the later government belong in the account. Neither erases the other.

title: The reservation clip and its missing condition
claim: At Georgetown, Rahul Gandhi announced that Congress would scrap reservations on taking power.
summary: His answer discussed a hypothetical fair society and said India had not reached it.
context: Reporting on his September 2024 US visit recorded an answer about the future of reservations. The article date here is the reporting date, not a certified local event timestamp.
evidence: PTI’s account includes both parts: considering removal when India becomes fair, and his statement that it is not fair now. Alt News’s comparison locates the passage around 57:00 and reports that the latter qualification was omitted from the viral clip.
finding: Misleading. He did discuss conditional future removal, so saying he never mentioned it would also be inaccurate. The answer does not announce an immediate promise to abolish reservations after winning office.
limit: This assesses the circulated interpretation of that answer, not Congress’s entire policy record or a guarantee about future policy. It relies on PTI and the published comparison; original playback was not independently completed.
sources: PTI via Business Standard, Georgetown remarks, 10 September 2024
Alt News, clip comparison and context, 12 September 2024

history.scope: Relevant policy history; recording determines verdict
before_2014: UPA’s record included expanding the constitutional basis for educational reservation through the 93rd Amendment and legislating central-institution admission quotas. Reservations were therefore an established policy framework before the Georgetown remarks.

These measures do not prove a party will never change its future policy. Equally, a conditional answer in 2024 does not establish that Congress immediately repudiated its earlier legislation. The wording of the particular answer and its omitted condition still control this check.
history.comparison: The historical position supplies policy context, not a substitute for the recording. This check does not audit Congress’s entire reservation record at Union and state levels.
sources: India Code, Central Educational Institutions Act, 2006, sections 3–6

title: Agniveer payments: insurance received, ex gratia pending
claim: On 5 July 2024, Rahul Gandhi challenged the non-payment of ex-gratia benefits to Agniveer Ajay Kumar’s family, distinguishing them from insurance.
summary: The narrow point about pending ex-gratia benefits is supported by the Army’s own statement. A claim of no money from any source would be wrong.
context: The dispute developed across several statements. On 5 July, PTI reported Gandhi explicitly distinguishing insurance from compensation and asking why ex-gratia benefits had not been paid. This check assesses that specific point, rather than treating every statement during the dispute as identical.
evidence: Akashvani’s 4 July account of the Army clarification says ₹98.39 lakh had been paid and approximately ₹67 lakh in ex-gratia and other benefits remained due, subject to final settlement and verification. In a direct Indian Express interview published on 5 July, the father acknowledged ₹98 lakh in insurance receipts and said central ex-gratia had not arrived. The report also records ₹1 crore from the Punjab government.
finding: Supported for the narrow historical claim that central ex-gratia benefits were still pending at that stage. Insurance receipts do not prove that a separate ex-gratia payment was made. Conversely, the reported insurance and state payment mean money had already reached the family. Neither side’s wider wording should replace the payment-by-payment record.
limit: No bank statements, settlement order or later payment confirmation were inspected. This finding describes the early July 2024 record and does not establish what remains unpaid today. The Army statement is accessed through Akashvani’s report; Gandhi’s wording through PTI. The family interview independently supports the distinction, not an audit of every amount.
sources: PTI via Indian Express, Gandhi’s clarification, 5 July 2024
Indian Express, direct interview with the father, 5 July 2024

table.caption: Reported position in early July 2024. The pending ₹67 lakh includes several benefits, not ex gratia alone. Figures are attributed, not independently audited.
rows: ₹98.39 lakh, according to its clarification. This overlaps the insurance receipts; do not add the two.
Approximately ₹67 lakh still to be settled, according to the Army.
₹1 crore received, according to the father’s interview. Separate from the central benefits.

before_2014: A Defence Ministry reply of 7 August 2013, under UPA-II, separately listed family pension, death gratuity, ex-gratia and Army Group Insurance among benefits for eligible families. Insurance and ex-gratia were therefore distinct categories before the present dispute.

Agnipath was introduced in 2022. Its four-year Agniveer engagement and package differ from the earlier regular-cadre model, including on pension and gratuity. A fair comparison requires the deceased person’s engagement type, casualty classification, eligibility and actual disbursement dates.
history.comparison: The pre-2014 record supports separating payment categories, not comparing one headline lump sum with another. It does not prove that all eligible UPA-era families received timely payments, nor establish what Ajay Kumar’s family received after July 2024.

title: A constitution question with an inserted reaction
claim: A parliamentary clip showed Gandhi unable to answer Anurag Thakur’s question about the Constitution.
summary: The comparison shows Gandhi was absent when that passage was delivered.
context: AFP traced the footage to Sansad TV’s recording of Thakur’s 1 July 2024 speech. The viral edit presents a reaction as if it occurred in response to the question.
evidence: AFP locates the relevant remarks at 56:36 and a view of the opposition benches at 56:47, where Gandhi is not in his seat. Its account documents the opposition walkout and the manipulation of the circulating clip.
finding: False as evidence that Gandhi was present and stumped by that question. A cutaway cannot establish a contemporaneous reaction when the original sequence shows his absence.
limit: This relies on AFP’s published comparison; full original playback was not independently completed. It does not establish Gandhi’s knowledge of any constitutional provision.
sources: AFP, Sansad TV sequence comparison, July 2024

history.scope: Event-specific; no valid government-era performance comparison
before_2014: The footage concerns a July 2024 parliamentary speech and who was in the chamber at that moment. There is no comparable Congress-era baseline for a reaction that the edit inserts into a different sequence. No historical claim about Gandhi’s constitutional knowledge is established here.
history.comparison: A prior speech or a party’s pre-2014 constitutional record cannot authenticate this reaction shot. The original sequence, timing and attendance determine the verdict.
sources: AFP, Sansad TV sequence comparison, July 2024

title: The video that made him concede defeat
claim: A circulating video showed Rahul Gandhi predicting Modi’s victory during the 2024 campaign.
summary: The clip removed words and reversed the meaning of his speech.
context: The source speech was delivered in Kanpur on 10 May 2024. AFP traced the circulating clip to a Congress livestream and compared the relevant passages.
evidence: AFP’s comparison identifies a removed negation around 0:57. Another cut around 1:41 changes a prediction of at least 50 opposition seats in Uttar Pradesh into an apparent prediction of none.
finding: The viral clip does not faithfully represent the statement. His prediction of an opposition victory is separate from the question of whether the recording was manipulated.
limit: This assessment relies on AFP’s published comparison. Original video playback was not independently completed in this rebuild.

history.scope: Event-specific; no valid government-era performance comparison
before_2014: This check concerns a particular 2024 campaign recording, not an election-performance trend. No pre-2014 endorsement, concession or party position is being inferred. Historical election results would answer a different question from what was said in the clip.
history.comparison: The full passage and the editing determine whether this was a prediction of Modi’s victory. A Congress-era comparison would not establish the authenticity of the 2024 audio or sequence.

title: The red book was an Indian Constitution edition
claim: A rally photograph showed Rahul Gandhi displaying China’s constitution.
summary: Other photographs identify the book as a pocket edition of the Constitution of India.
context: AFP traced the photograph to a 5 May 2024 Telangana rally photo set posted by Revanth Reddy. The allegation relied in part on the red cover.
evidence: AFP’s comparison shows another view with the Indian title and EBC publisher mark visible. It also records the publisher’s confirmation that the book was its Indian Constitution pocket edition.
finding: False for the book in this photograph. Cover colour alone cannot identify the country whose constitution a book contains; different editions can have different covers.
limit: This relies on AFP’s published image comparison and publisher inquiry. The physical book was not inspected independently. It does not assess either party’s wider constitutional claims.
sources: AFP, photo comparison and publisher confirmation, 3 June 2024

history.scope: Event-specific; no valid government-era performance comparison
before_2014: This allegation concerns a book held at a May 2024 rally. A comparison with Congress governments before 2014 cannot identify the volume in that photograph. The useful historical distinction is between the Constitution itself and the many editions in which it is printed, not a party’s ownership of the text.
history.comparison: The visible title and publisher confirmation identify this edition. Neither cover colour nor a party’s past relationship with China can substitute for that evidence.
sources: AFP, photo comparison and publisher confirmation, 3 June 2024

title: A Pakistan shop recast as a Wayanad temple
claim: Rahul Gandhi inaugurated a chicken shop in a Hindu temple in Wayanad.
summary: The circulated footage shows a location in Pakistan, not an inauguration in Wayanad.
context: The video circulated during the 2024 election campaign with an Indian location and Gandhi connection added to its caption.
evidence: AFP traced the footage to an August 2023 upload about a shop in front of the defunct Seeta Ram temple in Ahmadpur Sial, Punjab, Pakistan. It compared location features and obtained corroboration from a Pakistani Hindu activist.
finding: False for the location and Gandhi-inauguration claim. The identified source does not show the alleged Wayanad event.
limit: This entry relies on AFP’s documented tracing and comparison; full original-video playback was not independently repeated here. It does not audit the building’s complete ownership or legal history.

history.scope: Historical context: establish the original event before making a political comparison.
before_2014: The source footage predates the 2024 Indian election claim. AFP’s interviewee placed the building in the wider history of temples left without congregations after Partition in 1947. That is attributed background, not a complete archival history of this particular property. A claim about a Pakistan building cannot be established by citing the record of a Congress government in India before 2014.
history.comparison: The decisive historical comparison is between the earlier Pakistan upload and the later Wayanad caption. It identifies a miscaptioned location rather than a change in Indian temple policy.

review_note: Reviewed 18 October 2026 (IST). Initial publication. Historical context included.

title: The appeal to vote for BJP was doctored
claim: Rahul Gandhi urged voters to support Narendra Modi and BJP instead of Congress in an April 2024 video.
summary: The original appeal supported Congress. The circulating version reversed the message.
context: AFP traced this recording to Gandhi’s official YouTube upload dated 25 April 2024. This check concerns that appeal, separately from the site’s other edited election-speech example.
evidence: AFP’s side-by-side account shows the original blaming BJP and RSS for attacks on democracy while presenting Congress and INDIA as defenders. The original ends by asking voters to support Congress and its hand symbol; the doctored version substitutes a pro-Modi message.
finding: False for this supposed endorsement. The edit changes both the parties being criticised and the party voters are asked to support.
limit: This relies on AFP’s published comparison; complete original playback was not independently completed. Restoring the original appeal does not verify the political accusations or campaign promises within it.
sources: AFP, original appeal and doctored version, 4 June 2024; updated 6 June

history.scope: Event-specific; no valid government-era performance comparison
before_2014: The underlying source was published on 25 April 2024. This is a claim about a specific electoral appeal, rather than about Congress’s pre-2014 policy. No historical alliance, rivalry or earlier public statement authenticates a newly edited endorsement.
history.comparison: Evaluate the original and circulating versions side by side. The missing or substituted words determine which party the appeal supports, regardless of earlier party history.
sources: AFP, original appeal and doctored version, 4 June 2024; updated 6 June

title: Loan write-offs are not the same as loan waivers
claim: Rahul Gandhi said Modi had waived ₹16 lakh crore of loans for his billionaire friends.
summary: An aggregate bank write-off figure does not establish that borrowers’ debts were cancelled or identify who benefited.
context: PTI reported Gandhi’s 24 April 2024 Hindi post as alleging ₹16 lakh crore in loan waivers for billionaire friends. The check concerns the distinction between write-offs and waivers, and what a banking total establishes. It does not certify an alternative total or a list of recipients.
evidence: RBI’s 8 June 2023 framework defines a technical write-off as an accounting action that leaves the claim against the borrower and the right to recover intact. It separately defines a compromise settlement, which involves an agreed settlement and may involve giving up part of a claim. The regulator’s distinction was already in force when Gandhi made the statement.
finding: Treating bank write-offs as proof of government loan forgiveness is misleading. Write-off data alone cannot establish ₹16 lakh crore of cancelled liabilities, a government order cancelling them, or that all recipients were billionaires. This does not show that every written-off loan was recovered or that banks suffered no losses. Low recoveries and the fairness of settlements remain valid questions requiring their own evidence.
limit: The precise ₹16 lakh crore total, its period, the mix of write-offs and settlements, and the alleged beneficiaries were not independently reconstructed in this check. Some settlements do reduce a borrower’s liability. Do not assume every accounting write-off is a technical write-off without inspecting the underlying account. Attribution relies on PTI’s report; the original X post was not independently retrieved.
sources: PTI via Business Standard, Gandhi’s post, 24 April 2024
RBI, Framework for Compromise Settlements and Technical Write-offs, 8 June 2023, Annex paragraph 1

table.caption: Different actions, different effects. An account-level record is needed to establish which occurred.
rows: Removed from the lender’s accounts for accounting purposes; borrower remains liable.
Negotiated settlement; lender may give up part of its claim.
Lender gives up the relevant repayment claim. A write-off total alone does not establish this.

before_2014: Bank write-offs were not invented after 2014. RBI’s July 2013 prudential circular already discussed loss-asset write-offs and required management information on technical write-offs. This is a regulatory practice that existed under UPA, not evidence that every loan written off then was forgiven.

A genuine waiver also existed: the 2008 agricultural debt-waiver scheme. Its original rules explicitly extinguished eligible small and marginal farmers’ dues and offered conditional relief to other farmers. That is legally different from removing a bad asset from a bank’s balance sheet while retaining recovery rights.
history.comparison: Apply the same terminology across governments. To compare performance, also examine recoveries, originating loan dates and total advances, rather than attributing every later write-off to loans first granted in that government’s term.
sources: RBI, July 2013 prudential circular, sections 5.2 and 8 and information systems
Finance Ministry, original debt-waiver guidelines, 23 May 2008

title: Money for scrolling? The missing apprenticeship proposal
claim: Rahul Gandhi promised unemployed youth monthly payments for watching Instagram and Facebook.
summary: The clipped passage removed the proposal for paid training.
context: The source was his 20 April 2024 Bihar campaign speech. AFP traced the circulating excerpt to the longer livestream and compared the passages.
evidence: AFP identifies the explanation of a right to apprenticeship around 9:33 and the circulating excerpt around 12:33. He was describing young people who would move from joblessness into training, rather than making social-media viewing the paid work. Congress’s manifesto separately specifies a one-year apprenticeship for eligible diploma holders and graduates.
finding: Misleading as a description of the proposal. The reference to scrolling concerned the young people’s existing situation. It was not the activity for which the proposed apprenticeship payment would be made.
limit: This relies on AFP’s published video comparison and the manifesto. Full original playback was not independently completed. It does not assess delivery, funding or every eligibility detail.

history.scope: Earlier training framework; no claim of identical entitlement
before_2014: Paid apprenticeship was not a new idea in 2024. During UPA-II, the Labour Ministry’s March 2012 reply discussed the existing Apprentices Act, 1961 and proposed changes to its administration. Formal workplace training therefore predates this campaign proposal.

The 2024 manifesto proposed a particular expanded entitlement and payment. Existing apprenticeship arrangements do not establish that every eligible graduate already enjoyed that proposed right before 2014, or that Congress’s later proposal had been funded and delivered.
history.comparison: The useful historical comparison is eligibility, places, stipend and employer obligations. It provides no basis for turning the clipped reference to unemployed people scrolling into a promise to pay them for scrolling.
sources: Labour Ministry, existing Apprentices Act and proposed changes, 19 March 2012

title: 22 people and 70 crore citizens: an unreproduced comparison
claim: Twenty-two wealthy Indians held as much wealth as 70 crore other Indians combined.
summary: The statement is documented. A dated, reproducible calculation for this exact equality was not obtained.
context: Mint reported the comparison from Gandhi’s 20 April 2024 Amroha rally. The report establishes attribution, rather than supplying the wealth calculation.
evidence: The reviewed account does not identify all 22 people, a common valuation date, the precise population group on the other side, or a dataset and calculation reconciling their wealth. General evidence of high inequality does not establish this exact numerical equality.
finding: Unverified for the specific 22-versus-70-crore comparison. Lack of a reproduced calculation is not proof that the comparison is false.
limit: Needed: a defined wealth measure, named or consistently ranked holdings, treatment of liabilities and households, and compatible population estimates at one reference date. His separate allegations about bank money, GST and demonetisation are not assessed here.

before_2014: High and rising inequality predates 2014. The World Inequality Report 2018’s India series estimates the top 1% income share at about 6% in 1982–83, 15% in 2000 and 23% in 2014. These years span Congress-led and other governments.

Those are estimated income shares, not the wealth held by 22 named people. A rise already underway before 2014 means the entire pattern cannot be assigned to one later administration from timing alone. The report’s historical estimates also carry data and modelling limitations.
history.comparison: The earlier trend adds context but cannot validate the exact 22-versus-70-crore wealth equality. Income, net wealth, adult populations and total populations must remain separate measures.

title: A survey speech edited to mention minorities alone
claim: A Hyderabad clip showed Gandhi proposing surveys and rights exclusively for minorities.
summary: The longer passage also names backward classes, Dalits, Adivasis and poor general-category people.
context: The passage comes from the Congress manifesto launch in Hyderabad on 6 April 2024. The party’s event page confirms the occasion and date.
evidence: Alt News’s comparison identifies the relevant passage around 31:54. It reports that the circulated version removes the other named groups and retains minorities, changing the apparent scope of his proposal.
finding: Misleading for the claim of exclusive minority beneficiaries. The omission is material to who the speech addresses. Restoring those words does not by itself settle every debate about wealth redistribution, taxation or the proposed surveys.
limit: This relies on the published contextual comparison. The original full recording was not independently played, and the practical design of the proposed measures is outside this check.
sources: Alt News, comparison of the edited passage, 23 April 2024

before_2014: UPA’s 2011 Socio-Economic and Caste Census was an earlier attempt to collect household and social information for policy. The Cabinet’s September 2010 decision distinguished separate caste enumeration from the main population census.

That history does not establish that the 2024 speech proposed an identical exercise, still less that it promised confiscation or benefits only for minorities. The original passage names multiple social groups. Design, legal authority and intended uses need to be checked separately for each survey.
history.comparison: Earlier data collection provides context for the proposal. The verdict on the clip concerns the removal of named beneficiary groups, not whether every survey proposal is good policy.
sources: Rural Development Ministry, SECC launch and progress, 2011 review

title: 83% of the unemployed were young: the denominator matters
claim: Young people accounted for about 83% of India’s unemployed population in the cited employment report.
summary: The ILO–IHD report gives 82.9% for 2022. That is a share of the unemployed, not a youth unemployment rate.
context: PTI’s 27 March 2024 report specifically attributes the 83% statement to Rahul Gandhi. The verdict applies only to this statistic, rather than every claim in that statement.
evidence: India Employment Report 2024, printed page 90, figure 4.10, reports that youths made up 82.9% of unemployed persons in 2022 under usual principal and subsidiary status. The report uses ages 15–29 for youth. Rounding 82.9 to a whole percentage gives 83.
finding: Supported with the original year and denominator retained. It does not mean 83 out of every 100 young Indians were unemployed. Low-paid people who are working must not automatically be added to the unemployed category.
limit: This is a historical report-based statistic, not a 2026 estimate. Gandhi’s separate wording about 65% educated youth and Congress’s proposed remedies are outside this verdict.
sources: PTI via Devdiscourse, Rahul Gandhi statement, 27 March 2024
ILO–IHD, India Employment Report 2024, printed page 90, figure 4.10 (PDF page 124)

before_2014: The same ILO–IHD figure places young people’s share of the unemployed at 87.1% in 2012, during UPA-II, compared with 82.9% in 2022. The historical comparison therefore shows youth already dominated unemployment before 2014.

A lower share does not necessarily mean a lower youth unemployment rate or more youth jobs. The denominator is all unemployed people, and both the age distribution of the workforce and unemployment among older workers affect it.
history.comparison: The 83% statistic is supported for 2022, but does not prove that this concentration first appeared after 2014 or worsened from the 2012 share. Separate rate and employment data are needed to assess labour-market performance.
sources: ILO–IHD, India Employment Report 2024, figure 4.10, printed page 90

title: The warning concerned institutions, not Hindus
claim: A video showed Gandhi threatening Hindus with action once the BJP government lost power.
summary: The original passage was about alleged institutional misconduct in the electoral-bonds controversy.
context: AFP traced the clip to a 15 March 2024 Maharashtra press conference, although it circulated with the Hindu-targeting claim in November.
evidence: AFP identifies the preceding passage around 18:04: Gandhi names the Election Commission, CBI and ED and accuses them of serving BJP and RSS. Around 18:34 he warns of action after a change of government. The missing preceding words identify the target of that warning.
finding: False as a description of a threat to Hindus in this recording. Replacing the institutional referent with a religious community materially changes the statement.
limit: This relies on AFP’s contextual comparison; original full playback was not independently completed. It does not verify Gandhi’s accusations against institutions or decide whether his warning was appropriate.

history.scope: Funding background; specific warning has its own context
before_2014: Electoral funding had a regulated but imperfect disclosure framework before electoral bonds. The pre-bond corporate rules included a 7.5% average-profit ceiling and donor disclosures above specified thresholds, as described by PRS. These rules also applied to parties other than BJP.

Electoral bonds were announced in 2017 and notified in 2018, after UPA. This creates a real policy discontinuity, but does not itself verify Gandhi’s accusations of institutional collusion or his proposed response to it.
history.comparison: The historical funding framework helps explain the press conference’s subject. Whether the warning targeted institutions or Hindus is settled by the surrounding words, not by comparing Congress’s and BJP’s funding records.
sources: PRS, pre-bond corporate contributions and disclosure framework, December 2016
PRS, electoral-bond scheme notified in January 2018

title: Thirty lakh vacancies: what was being counted?
claim: Rahul Gandhi said there were 30 lakh government vacancies and pledged to fill them if elected.
summary: The pledge is documented. The reviewed sources do not supply an auditable total of 30 lakh distinct vacant posts.
context: At Banswara on 7 March 2024, Gandhi said Congress had counted 30 lakh government vacancies, according to contemporaneous Indian Express reporting. The April manifesto repeated the figure and listed central government posts, educational and medical institutions, and the Central Armed Police Forces. This check tests the claimed vacancy count, not whether a future government would fulfil the pledge.
evidence: Lok Sabha answer 1093, dated 26 July 2023, reports 9,64,359 vacant regular civilian Union government posts as of 1 March 2022. In a separate Indian Express interview, Congress manifesto committee member Praveen Chakravarty acknowledged about 9.6 lakh central vacancies and said additional sectors brought the total to 30 lakh. That interview explains the party’s intended scope but supplies no itemised calculation.
finding: The official figure is older and has a defined employee category. It does not, by itself, refute the broader campaign total. Equally, listing additional sectors does not verify their numbers or establish that they do not overlap with the official count. The claim remains unverified on the evidence reviewed.
limit: Required to settle the claim: an institution-by-institution list, a common reference date, sanctioned and filled strengths, and removal of duplicate posts. Original rally footage was not independently played. No verdict on the promise’s feasibility or delivery is assigned.
sources: Indian Express, manifesto committee interview, 7 March 2024

table.caption: Different dates and coverage. These figures are not a like-for-like comparison.

before_2014: A UPA-II parliamentary reply published on 11 December 2013 estimated 6,00,013 vacant regular Central Government civilian posts as at 1 March 2012. The same reply described a September 2013 economy instruction limiting revival of posts vacant for over a year.

The later official record used in this check reports 9,64,359 such vacancies as at 1 March 2022. These two stocks show vacancies existed under both governments. They do not by themselves validate Congress’s broader 30-lakh count, which includes additional institutions and sectors.
history.comparison: The historical and later official civilian counts have a narrower scope than the campaign total. Changes in sanctioned strength, departmental coverage and the treatment of abolished posts still need checking before attributing the difference to recruitment policy alone.
sources: Personnel Ministry, 11 December 2013, vacancies as at 1 March 2012

title: “Twice Pakistan’s unemployment”: youth or everyone?
claim: India’s unemployment was roughly double Pakistan’s, with about 23% of youth unemployed in India and 12% in Pakistan.
summary: Contemporaneous reporting supports a youth-specific comparison. The exact historical data vintage was not independently recovered.
context: Reports of Gandhi’s 3 March 2024 Gwalior speech include the youth figures alongside his broader wording. Assessing only the headline would omit an important qualification.
evidence: Times of India reported 2022 World Bank youth estimates of 23.22% for India and 11.3% for Pakistan, roughly a two-to-one ratio. FRED defines that World Bank indicator as the unemployed share of the labour force aged 15–24. Its currently displayed, revised 2022 India value is 17.732%, illustrating why the release vintage matters.
finding: The reported historical youth figures broadly support his rounded comparison. They do not establish that India’s unemployment rate for the whole workforce was double Pakistan’s. The exact vintage remains unverified in this review; revised data alone do not prove the original statement false.
limit: The original pre-speech dataset and full recording were not independently obtained. Do not mix youth and all-age rates, national and modelled estimates, or different release vintages. This is not a current cross-country comparison.
sources: Times of India, Gwalior statement and reported 2022 estimates, 3 March 2024
FRED, World Bank indicator SL.UEM.1524.ZS, definition and revised observations

before_2014: Youth unemployment was a concern before 2014, but a valid India–Pakistan comparison requires both countries’ same-year, same-vintage estimates for the same age band. This review has not recovered a matched pre-2014 World Bank vintage alongside the vintage Gandhi appears to have cited.

The ILO–IHD report contains India’s historical employment series, but its 15–29 definition is not interchangeable with the World Bank 15–24 youth indicator discussed here. Substituting one for the other would manufacture a before-and-after trend.
history.comparison: No numerical Congress-era cross-country ratio is asserted. The pre-2014 comparison remains an identified evidence gap, rather than a reason to pronounce either government better on an unmatched measure.
sources: ILO–IHD, India Employment Report 2024, figure 4.10, printed page 90

title: 50 + 15 = 73? The omitted eight
claim: A viral video showed Rahul Gandhi incorrectly adding 50 and 15 to get 73.
summary: The longer passage includes another eight. The arithmetic is 50 + 15 + 8 = 73.
context: Newschecker traced the excerpt to a longer Congress post dated 8 February 2024 about a speech in Odisha. The displayed date is that source’s publication date.
evidence: Its comparison identifies three population-share figures in the longer statement, with the eight referring to tribal communities. Omitting that term creates the apparent arithmetic error.
finding: False for this purported mathematical mistake. Restoring the missing term makes the sum correct. That does not independently verify the population percentages he cited.
limit: The verdict concerns editing and arithmetic, not a census-based demographic finding. This review relies on Newschecker’s published comparison; full original playback was not independently completed.
sources: Congress source post dated 8 February 2024, identified by Newschecker; playback not independently completed

before_2014: The population-measurement issue predates 2014. The UPA Cabinet’s 2010 decision acknowledged the lack of a detailed published all-caste census since 1931 and authorised a separate enumeration. The regular census continued collecting SC and ST information.

That background explains why demographic assertions require a dated source and defined categories. It does not supply a verified 50% OBC estimate, or prove that population shares remained fixed across decades.
history.comparison: The arithmetic is correct once the missing eight is restored. Verifying the percentages would be a different claim, requiring evidence beyond either the edited clip or a historical survey announcement.

title: Three OBC secretaries out of 90: where is the roster?
claim: Only three of the Union government’s 90 secretaries belonged to OBC communities.
summary: The official debate confirms he made the claim. It does not independently establish the count.
context: Gandhi made the statement during the women’s reservation debate on 20 September 2023. The Lok Sabha transcript records his description of 90 secretaries and his count of three OBC officers on printed pages 207–209.
evidence: A parliamentary transcript is primary evidence of the words spoken, not verification of the speaker’s underlying research. The dated officer list and the community classification records needed to reproduce the count were not obtained.
finding: Unverified for the count at that date. This is a specific claim about a senior group, not a statistic for the entire civil service. Broader workforce representation figures or lists from other years would not settle it.
limit: Needed: a same-date definition and roster of secretary-level posts, treatment of equivalent ranks and vacancies, and an authoritative classification source. Community identities must not be guessed from names. His separate claim about control of 5% of the budget is outside this verdict.
sources: Lok Sabha debate, 20 September 2023, printed pages 207–209 (PDF pages 208–210)

before_2014: The government later reported OBC representation of 19.28% across posts and services in 71 ministries/departments as at 1 January 2014, near the end of UPA-II. It noted that OBC reservation started in 1993 and that pre-1993 appointees were not counted in that category.

That administrative baseline is not a count of OBC officers among secretaries. Senior-rank representation reflects earlier recruitment cohorts, promotion and empanelment as well as the current appointment process. Implementation in 1993 fell during P. V. Narasimha Rao’s Congress government, before UPA’s 2004–14 tenure.
history.comparison: An all-service percentage cannot verify or rebut “three out of 90” at secretary level. A same-rank pre-2014 roster and a 2023 roster with authoritative classifications are still required.
sources: Personnel Ministry, representation as at 1 January 2014, reported 2016
PMO, P. V. Narasimha Rao’s 1991–96 tenure

title: Did the 2023 women’s quota depend on a new census?
claim: The women’s reservation proposal required a new census and delimitation before the reserved seats would take effect.
summary: Yes. Those steps appear in the enacted 2023 text.
context: During the 20 September debate, Gandhi questioned both conditions and urged immediate implementation. His description of the conditions is a factual claim; his proposed alternative and suspicion about delay are separate arguments.
evidence: The official transcript records both objections on printed page 206. Section 5 of the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 inserted Article 334A. Its original text links the reserved seats to a delimitation exercise after publication of relevant figures from the first census following commencement.
finding: Supported as a description of the 2023 proposal and enacted mechanism. It does not establish the motive for the conditions or a guaranteed implementation year.
limit: This is a historical reading of the September 2023 text. It does not certify subsequent legislative changes, today’s implementation timetable, or the feasibility of Gandhi’s immediate-implementation alternative.
sources: Lok Sabha debate, 20 September 2023, printed page 206 (PDF page 207)
Legislative Department, Gazette copy, 106th Amendment Act, section 5, page 2

before_2014: Under UPA, the 2008 women’s reservation bill sought a one-third quota in the Lok Sabha and state Assemblies. It passed the Rajya Sabha in 2010, but did not pass the Lok Sabha and lapsed with the 15th Lok Sabha. Earlier attempts in 1996, 1998 and 1999 also failed to become law.

The 2008 proposal used rotation after general elections; the 2023 proposal ties rotation to delimitation and includes the census/delimitation activation mechanism examined here. Passing one chamber in the UPA period did not reserve those seats in actual elections.
history.comparison: Credit the earlier legislative effort while recording its non-enactment. The 2023 law’s existence and its deferred activation are separate facts. Neither the previous failure nor the later enactment establishes motive.
sources: PRS, history of women’s reservation proposals and 2008/2023 comparison

title: The MGNREGA allocation cut in Budget 2023
claim: The government reduced the MGNREGA budget allocation for 2023–24.
summary: The initial allocation fell. The percentage depends on whether the comparison uses the previous original or revised estimate.
context: The ministry’s February 2023 rebuttal identifies a Gandhi Facebook post criticising the budget reduction. This checks the allocation, rather than every allegation in that dispute.
evidence: Budget 2023–24 set MGNREGA at ₹60,000 crore. The previous year’s original estimate was ₹73,000 crore and its revised estimate ₹89,400 crore. The reductions are therefore about 17.8% and 32.9%, respectively. Later budget documents revised the 2023–24 allocation upward to ₹86,000 crore.
finding: Supported for the initial budget reduction. A claim about a roughly one-third cut needs to identify the revised-estimate baseline. The initial allocation is not the final annual expenditure.
limit: A demand-driven scheme can receive supplementary funding. That mechanism neither guarantees that every request is met promptly nor proves that actual annual spending fell by the initial percentage.
sources: Rural Development Ministry: response to Gandhi’s February 2023 post
Union Budget 2023–24: major schemes, MGNREGA row
Union Budget 2024–25: Rural Development demand, revised allocation

history.scope: Before 2014: compare the same budget stage and account for prices.
before_2014: The UPA’s 2013–14 Budget at a Glance allocated ₹33,000 crore to MGNREGA. This is one specific original-budget baseline, not a claim that no earlier UPA budget was higher. Comparing that nominal figure with a budget ten years later requires inflation, wage rates, work demand and final expenditure to assess purchasing power or adequacy. The existence of a later nominally larger allocation does not disprove a year-on-year cut.
history.comparison: Both statements can be true: the NDA’s initial 2023–24 allocation exceeded the UPA’s 2013–14 nominal allocation and was lower than the preceding NDA year’s allocation. The immediate claim concerns the latter comparison.
sources: Union Budget 2013–14: major schemes, MGNREGA row

review_note: Reviewed 18 October 2026 (IST). Initial publication. Historical context included.

title: An explicit soundtrack added to a Jaipur concert
claim: Rahul Gandhi watched a performer sing the explicit song heard in a viral concert clip.
summary: The event was real, but AFP found that the circulated soundtrack had been replaced.
context: The scene came from the concert marking 100 days of the Bharat Jodo Yatra at Jaipur’s Albert Hall in December 2022.
evidence: AFP compared the viral clip with longer event footage. It identified Sunidhi Chauhan performing Right Here Right Now, from the 2005 film Bluffmaster, in the original scene. The circulated version substituted an explicit Bhojpuri song.
finding: False for the song attributed to that performance. The genuine presence of Gandhi at the concert does not authenticate the replacement audio.
limit: The assessment follows AFP’s original-source comparison. Full concert playback and independent audio forensics were not repeated here. No song lyrics are reproduced.

history.scope: Historical context: establish the original event before making a political comparison.
before_2014: The original performance took place on 16 December 2022, before the manipulated version was checked in January 2023. The identified original song’s 2005 release is cultural provenance, not evidence about a government’s conduct. A Congress-era policy comparison before 2014 would not determine what was sung at this later concert. The relevant comparison keeps the same event and checks its original soundtrack.
history.comparison: Historical context identifies the concert and source music. The verdict concerns the substituted audio, without inferring wrongdoing from attendance at the genuine event.

review_note: Reviewed 18 October 2026 (IST). Initial publication. Historical context included.

title: Senior rail concessions were withdrawn
claim: Senior citizens had lost their railway fare concession under the Modi government.
summary: The withdrawal is documented. This check concerns the concession, not the other spending comparisons in the same post.
context: Gandhi criticised the absence of senior concessions in July 2022. The relevant policy change began during the pandemic in March 2020.
evidence: The Railway Ministry announcement withdrew concessions from 20 March 2020 until further advisory, retaining specified exceptions for patients, students and persons with disabilities. Senior concessions were among those withdrawn. PTI reported Gandhi’s July 2022 criticism of their continued absence.
finding: Supported for the withdrawal of the senior-citizen concession. The policy’s stated pandemic rationale does not change the fact that the discount was removed.
limit: The figures for advertising, aircraft and corporate tax relief in the accompanying political comparison are outside this check. This entry does not establish the policy’s status in October 2026.

history.scope: Before 2014: the UPA expanded an existing concession.
before_2014: In May 2011, the UPA Railway Ministry announced that men aged 60 and above would receive a 40% concession instead of 30%. For women, it reduced the qualifying age from 60 to 58 while retaining the 50% concession. These changes took effect on 1 June 2011. The announcement describes an enhancement, so the UPA should not be credited here with creating the entire senior-concession system.
history.comparison: The documented comparison is an expansion under the UPA in 2011 and withdrawal under the NDA in 2020. It does not by itself establish the fiscal cost or the merits of every possible restoration model.

review_note: Reviewed 18 October 2026 (IST). Initial publication. Historical context included.

title: Were packaged milk, curd and butter all taxed at 5%?
claim: Packaged milk, curd and butter would now attract 5% GST.
summary: The July 2022 rules did not put all these products in a single 5% bracket.
context: PTI reported a broader food-tax list in Gandhi’s Facebook post. This check isolates its milk, curd and butter examples under the July 2022 rules.
evidence: A 25 July 2022 parliamentary answer says fresh and pasteurised milk were fully exempt. UHT milk attracted 5%. Pre-packaged and labelled curd attracted 5%, while unpackaged curd was exempt. Butter attracted 12%. The ministry’s food FAQ also explains that some branded packaged foods already attracted tax before the labelling-rule change.
finding: Misleading as a blanket 5% description. It combines exempt goods and goods with different rates, and obscures the distinction between packaging and the relevant product category.
limit: This is a historical July 2022 rate check. It does not claim these are the rates in October 2026, or decide every other food item in the original list.
sources: PTI / New Indian Express: Gandhi’s food-tax post, 19 July 2022
Lok Sabha answer, 25 July 2022: milk and dairy GST rates
Finance Ministry: pre-packaged and labelled food FAQ, 18 July 2022

history.scope: Before 2014: GST was proposed under the UPA but implemented later.
before_2014: The GST Council’s historical account traces the Union proposal to 2006. The UPA introduced the 115th Constitutional Amendment Bill in 2011, but it lapsed with the dissolution of the Lok Sabha in May 2014. The constitutional amendment was enacted under the NDA in 2016 and GST launched in 2017. Pre-GST India still had indirect taxes; the absence of GST is not proof that all food was tax-free.
history.comparison: The UPA helped develop the proposed framework, while the July 2022 classifications belong to the later GST system. This review has not reconstructed every state’s pre-2014 VAT treatment of each dairy product.
sources: GST Council: The GST Saga, legislative history

review_note: Reviewed 18 October 2026 (IST). Initial publication. Historical context included.

title: The “children” remark was about office vandals
claim: A video showed Rahul Gandhi calling the Udaipur murder suspects children and asking that they be forgiven.
summary: The recording concerned the vandalism of his Wayanad office.
context: The clip circulated in July 2022 after the killing of Kanhaiya Lal in Udaipur. AFP traced the original remarks to Gandhi’s response to a different incident.
evidence: AFP’s comparison identifies the subject as students who vandalised his constituency office. It also records a correction and apology by the television anchor whose broadcast linked the remarks to Udaipur.
finding: False for what this video depicts. Reassigning the subject of the remarks changes their meaning. The recording does not substantiate sympathy for the Udaipur murder suspects.
limit: This finding applies to the specific recording, not every statement Gandhi has made about violence. It relies on AFP’s published comparison and reported correction; full original playback was not independently completed.
sources: AFP, original-context investigation and broadcaster correction, 11 July 2022

history.scope: Event-specific; no valid government-era performance comparison
before_2014: The two incidents being conflated belong to 2022: the Wayanad office vandalism and the Udaipur killing. A pre-2014 record of a party’s responses to violence would not identify which incident Gandhi was discussing in this recording. No systematic cross-government comparison of those responses was completed.
history.comparison: The relevant history is the sequence of these two events and the broadcaster’s correction. This clip does not establish a general position on religious violence or a verdict on any government’s full record.
sources: AFP, original-context investigation and broadcaster correction, 11 July 2022

title: LPG: ₹410 to ₹885, with the subsidy context
claim: A domestic LPG cylinder cost about ₹410 in 2014 and about ₹885 in September 2021.
summary: The rounded Delhi prices are supported. The earlier amount was a subsidised consumer price, not the market cost of the gas.
context: Congress’s published account and contemporaneous reporting attribute this comparison to Gandhi’s 1 September 2021 briefing.
evidence: Contemporaneous PTI reporting identifies ₹410.50 for a 14.2-kg Delhi refill on 1 March 2014. The ministry’s historical table gives ₹884.50 from 1 September 2021. The increase between these selected nominal prices is about 115.47%.
finding: Supported for these dated Delhi consumer-price points. It is not an all-India price or an inflation-adjusted affordability measure. Subsidy eligibility and the difference between invoice and effective consumer cost matter.
limit: This does not audit every household’s bank-credit subsidy or establish that falling crude oil alone should determine LPG prices. The comparison is historical, not a current refill quote.
sources: PTI via Financial Express, March 2014 and September 2021 LPG prices
Petroleum Ministry, historical LPG price table, 4 August 2022

before_2014: Under UPA-II, the 2013 petroleum-pricing expert report listed a subsidised Delhi LPG price of ₹410.50 per cylinder and a much higher desired retail price at international-product prices. The gap was supported through subsidy and under-recovery arrangements.

Thus the lower pre-2014 consumer price was real, but did not mean LPG cost the economy only ₹410.50 to supply. Comparing affordability requires the household’s effective payment, income and usage, while fiscal comparisons must include the subsidy burden.
history.comparison: The subsidy context qualifies the reason for the price difference without erasing the rise paid by consumers at the selected dates. City, cylinder size, eligibility and inflation must stay visible.

title: Fuel prices at UPA’s exit: the dates do not quite match
claim: When UPA left office in 2014, Delhi petrol cost ₹71.51 a litre and diesel ₹57.28.
summary: Those prices appear in the official table, but their effective dates were in June 2014, after the change of government.
context: Congress’s published briefing gives these exact historical figures in Gandhi’s comparison with September 2021 prices.
evidence: PPAC’s IOC Delhi series shows petrol at ₹71.41 from 16 April 2014 and diesel at ₹56.71 from 16 May. The ₹57.28 diesel point starts on 1 June 2014; ₹71.51 petrol starts on 7 June. UPA left office in May, not June.
finding: Misleading on the precise attribution of both prices to UPA’s exit. The numerical difference is small and does not overturn the broad fact that the selected September 2021 prices were higher.
limit: This verdict is about baseline timing. It does not isolate the effects of excise, state VAT, exchange rates, international product prices or company margins. The figures are Delhi nominal prices, not national averages.
sources: Congress, exact figures in Gandhi’s briefing
PPAC, Delhi petrol/diesel revision dates, April 2002–June 2017

before_2014: PPAC’s Delhi series records petrol and diesel at ₹33.71 and ₹21.74 on 1 April 2004, before UPA took office. By the final UPA months the series was much higher. Fuel-price increases therefore occurred before as well as after 2014.

Petrol became market-determined in June 2010 under UPA; diesel did so in October 2014 under NDA. Regulation, subsidies and tax decisions differed across products and periods. Neither government’s price record can be explained by the crude-oil dollar price alone.
history.comparison: Use a genuine handover-date baseline for government comparisons, then separate policy effects from external costs. This article does not estimate a causal tax-versus-crude decomposition.
sources: PPAC, Delhi petrol/diesel revision dates, April 2002–June 2017
PPAC, dates of petrol and diesel price deregulation

table.caption: PPAC’s IOC Delhi price-revision table. Blank cells carry the preceding price until the next revision.

title: An Assam answer with its clarification removed
claim: An Assam participant rejected Gandhi’s suggestion that unemployment had increased.
summary: The short clip removes the participant’s subsequent clarification after translation.
context: The exchange took place at a student interaction in Lahowal, Dibrugarh, on 19 March 2021.
evidence: AFP compared the excerpt around 20:13–20:25 with the longer recording. The participant initially misunderstood the question. After clarification through translation, he said unemployment had increased. The viral excerpt leaves out that correction.
finding: Misleading. The initial response occurred, but omitting the clarification changes the meaning of the exchange.
limit: A participant’s answer is not a statistical measurement of Assam unemployment. This review relies on AFP’s longer-video comparison rather than independently repeating full playback.

history.scope: Historical context: establish the original event before making a political comparison.
before_2014: The source is a specific March 2021 conversation, not a survey of employment under successive governments. A meaningful comparison with Congress rule before 2014 would need Assam figures measured over comparable periods using the same age coverage and unemployment definition. This entry has not reconstructed that state series. The absence of such a comparison does not justify deleting the speaker’s clarification from the recorded exchange.
history.comparison: The original recording resolves what the participant answered. It leaves the separate question of Assam’s long-term employment performance open to properly matched statistical evidence.

title: Did Gandhi complain about unemployed eagles?
claim: Rahul Gandhi blamed the prime minister for unemployment among eagles.
summary: The viral sequence splices remarks about people’s jobs with a separate example involving birds and garbage.
context: Newschecker compared the viral edit with the longer February 2020 speech at Kondli in Delhi.
evidence: Its comparison places communal-climate remarks around 2:30, youth unemployment around 3:49, and the eagles-and-garbage passage around 10:07. Joining these passages makes a different statement from the one in the longer speech.
finding: False as a representation of what Gandhi said. The edited sequence does not substantiate the attributed claim about eagles needing employment.
limit: This assessment relies on Newschecker’s timestamped comparison. Full original playback was not independently repeated here. It does not verify the separate labour-market assertions made during the speech.

history.scope: Historical context: establish the original event before making a political comparison.
before_2014: The relevant historical document is the longer 5 February 2020 speech, whose passages precede their recombination into a viral joke. Gandhi’s record or Congress employment policy before 2014 cannot authenticate the joined sentence. A historical assessment of human unemployment would require a specified survey, age group and employment measure, rather than treating a manipulated bird reference as an economic statistic.
history.comparison: The comparison restores the sequence of the original remarks. It neither endorses the speech’s other arguments nor supplies evidence about employment under the UPA.
