title: What the Supreme Court did not say on Rafale
claim: The Supreme Court had endorsed the accusation behind Rahul Gandhi’s “chowkidar chor hai” slogan.
summary: The court did not make the finding attributed to it.
context: The April 2019 decision concerned consideration of documents in the Rafale review proceedings. It did not endorse Gandhi’s accusation against Narendra Modi.
evidence: Contemporaneous reporting of the November 2019 judgment records the court rejecting the attribution. It also records Gandhi’s unconditional apology and closure of the contempt proceedings with a caution.
finding: False on the narrow question of what the court said. This does not decide every allegation about the Rafale purchase or establish that Gandhi knowingly lied.
limit: This is a historical assessment of judicial attribution. The court-hosted PDF was inaccessible during this review; the finding relies on contemporaneous reporting of the judgment. A full recording of Gandhi’s remarks was not independently played.

before_2014: The fighter procurement process predates the 2014 change of government. A 2018 Defence Ministry response records Rafale’s selection as the lowest bidder and the start of negotiations in February 2012 for the earlier 126-aircraft MMRCA procurement.

That ministry response is an interested government account, especially when assigning blame for delay. The earlier negotiation and the subsequent 2016 contract should not be treated as identical packages without checking quantities, production arrangements and contractual terms.
history.comparison: The UPA procurement history matters to the wider Rafale controversy. It cannot make a 2019 Supreme Court order say something it did not say. Judicial attribution remains the narrow basis of the False verdict.
sources: Defence Ministry, chronology of earlier negotiations, 7 February 2018

title: Unemployment and the 45-year-high claim
claim: India’s unemployment rate had reached its highest level in 45 years.
summary: The official 2017–18 rate of 6.1% is confirmed. This review has not independently established the full 45-year ranking.
context: The January 2019 claim followed reporting on the then-unreleased PLFS. The government subsequently published the survey in May 2019.
evidence: MoSPI reported an all-ages unemployment rate of 6.1% under usual status, principal plus subsidiary activity, for 2017–18. This verifies that number. Establishing the historical superlative additionally requires a consistent series and treatment of the shift from the older Employment–Unemployment Surveys to PLFS. Officials raised survey-design comparability objections when releasing the figures.
finding: Unverified specifically for the complete 45-year ranking in this review. The confirmed 6.1% figure should not be treated as fabricated, and a methodological objection alone does not prove the historical claim false.
limit: The entire 1972–73 onward series has not been harmonised here. This is a limitation of this review, not evidence that another historical rate was higher.
sources: NDTV: official rate and comparability objection

history.scope: Before 2014: the UPA-era NSS baseline used a different survey programme.
before_2014: NSS Table 7 for 2011–12 reports an all-India, all-ages usual-status unemployment rate of 22 per 1,000 in the labour force, equivalent to 2.2%. It also reports different rates under principal status, weekly status and daily status. Choosing among these measures changes the comparison. The 2017–18 figure belongs to PLFS, so the change of survey design must accompany any comparison with the UPA-era observation.
history.comparison: The historical baseline shows that unemployment was measured before 2014 and that the cited usual-status rate was lower. It does not, without a harmonised series, independently settle a 45-year superlative.
sources: NSS: Employment and Unemployment 2011–12, Table 7, printed page 26

title: The UPA farm waiver: announcement versus reported benefit
claim: The UPA government waived farmers’ loans worth about ₹70,000 crore.
summary: A large waiver existed. The later official reported benefit was ₹52,259.86 crore, below the announced estimate.
context: PTI’s report of Gandhi’s 6 June 2018 Mandsaur rally records the ₹70,000-crore comparison. This check concerns the realised amount, not his separate ten-day promise for Madhya Pradesh.
evidence: The original 2008 Budget proposed a ₹60,000-crore scheme, subsequently expanded to an estimate around ₹71,680 crore. A 5 December 2014 parliamentary reply reports ₹52,259.86 crore benefiting 3.73 crore farmers. Announcement, estimated liability and reported benefit are different quantities.
finding: Misleading if ₹70,000 crore is presented as the final benefit delivered. It is a reasonable shorthand for the expanded announced scheme, but that qualification changes the claim materially.
limit: The later ministry total is an official reported aggregate, not a fresh account-level audit. It includes waiver and relief under the scheme. The additional assertion that the amount was a historical record is not assessed.
sources: PTI via NDTV, Mandsaur statement, 6 June 2018
Finance Minister, Cabinet decision and expanded scheme estimate, 23 May 2008

before_2014: UPA-I launched the scheme in 2008. The original rules covered eligible overdue institutional agricultural loans with specified disbursement and default dates. Small and marginal farmers received a full waiver of the eligible amount; other farmers received conditional relief, rather than every outstanding loan being cancelled.

The CAG examined implementation during the UPA period. Its description identifies the different beneficiary categories and implementing agencies. A scheme’s existence, its announced envelope and the extent of correct delivery are separate questions.
history.comparison: Use the reported delivered amount when comparing realised assistance across governments. Also compare eligibility, farmer coverage, inflation and credit conditions. A genuine agricultural waiver must not be equated with a bank’s technical write-off.
sources: Finance Ministry, original debt-waiver guidelines, 23 May 2008
CAG, 2013 performance audit of the 2008 debt-waiver scheme

title: Was ₹33,000 crore given away for the Nano?
claim: Narendra Modi gave Tata ₹33,000 crore for the Nano project.
summary: The precise total is not established here. A repayable loan cannot automatically be counted as an outright gift.
context: Gandhi used the Nano package in his 2017 Gujarat campaign. Contemporary reporting records Tata Motors disputing the description of the assistance.
evidence: Indian Express reported Tata’s statement that it had received a ₹584.8 crore loan from taxes paid by the Sanand plant, repayable under its agreement. That company response addresses a particular assistance component. It is not an independent valuation of land, infrastructure, tax treatment and all other possible benefits.
finding: Unverified for the ₹33,000 crore total and its presentation as money given away. The evidence inspected does not supply a complete audited package calculation.
limit: Tata is an interested party. Its rebuttal alone neither audits every benefit nor proves that the project received no subsidy. A concessional loan can contain a subsidy without its entire principal being a grant.
sources: Indian Express: Tata’s response to the ₹33,000 crore allegation

history.scope: Before 2014: a Gujarat state project during a UPA Union government.
before_2014: Tata announced the relocation of its Nano plant to Sanand in Gujarat in October 2008. Gujarat was governed by the BJP under Narendra Modi, while the Congress-led UPA governed at the Centre. The two governments must not be conflated. Evaluating a state incentive package requires its agreements and actual disbursements, rather than assigning every pre-2014 decision to Congress because it held Union office.
history.comparison: The historical issue is the state package’s terms and economic value. A full comparison would distinguish loan principal, repayment, interest subsidy and other concessions. This check has not reconstructed that complete valuation.
sources: Indian Express: Tata’s response to the ₹33,000 crore allegation
Tata Motors: Gujarat plant announcement, 7 October 2008

title: The potato-to-gold clip, with its missing context
claim: Rahul Gandhi promised a machine that turns potatoes into gold.
summary: He was mocking a promise he attributed to Modi, rather than making his own policy pledge.
context: The line comes from a November 2017 Gujarat campaign speech. Alt News reproduces the surrounding statement, including Gandhi’s attribution to Modi.
evidence: That context changes the meaning of the clipped passage. Alt News also found no public record supporting Gandhi’s attribution to Modi. A later edited Modi video is not proof of an original promise.
finding: Calling this Gandhi’s own promise is misleading. His claim that Modi made such a promise remains unsupported by the record reviewed.
limit: This assessment uses Alt News’s contextual comparison. The full original recording was not independently played during this rebuild.
sources: Alt News, context and edited counter-clip, 25 September 2020

history.scope: Event-specific; no valid government-era performance comparison
before_2014: The excerpt comes from a November 2017 Gujarat campaign speech. It is not evidence that a potato-to-gold machine featured in a UPA agricultural programme. No pre-2014 scheme or authentic earlier Modi promise matching that description was established by the reviewed contextual investigation.
history.comparison: There are two attribution tests: Gandhi was presenting the line as someone else’s claim, while his attribution to Modi still needs evidence. Neither a Congress farming record nor political satire verifies a real machine or an original promise.
sources: Alt News, context and edited counter-clip, 25 September 2020

title: Did roughly 99% of the banned cash return?
claim: Rahul Gandhi said RBI had reported that about 99% of the old currency had returned to banks.
summary: The rounded return figure is supported. It does not establish the source of the money or the intent behind demonetisation.
context: ANI’s report of Gandhi’s 8 September 2017 Parbhani speech attributes the 99% figure to him. The statement concerned the old ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes withdrawn in November 2016. His wider speech also alleged that demonetisation converted illicit money into legitimate money. That allegation is separate from the return percentage.
evidence: RBI’s 2017–18 currency-management chapter, paragraph VIII.20, records ₹15,310.73 billion returned after processing. Lok Sabha answer 4023 of 4 January 2019 gives both the reconciled original value, ₹15,417.93 billion, and the returned value. Dividing the latter by the former gives 99.3047%, or 99.3% rounded to one decimal place. These later records corroborate the broad numerical claim, rather than reproduce the provisional figures available at the 2017 speech.
finding: Supported for the narrow statement that approximately 99% of the specified notes returned, measured by value. A high return rate does not show that every deposit was lawful, that every illicit holding was identified, or that demonetisation was designed to help particular people. Those conclusions require separate evidence.
limit: The statement’s attribution relies on ANI’s contemporaneous report, not independent playback of the complete speech. The calculation uses later reconciled figures. It is not a verdict on the overall economic costs, benefits or legality of demonetisation.
sources: ANI via Business Standard, Parbhani speech, 8 September 2017
RBI Annual Report 2017–18, Currency Management, VIII.20
Lok Sabha answer 4023, 4 January 2019, parts (a) and (b)

table.caption: Reconciled figures published after the speech. Unit: ₹ billion.

before_2014: The closest late-UPA currency episode was RBI’s January 2014 withdrawal of pre-2005 banknote designs. Its 3 March 2014 circular explicitly retained their legal-tender status and provided full-value exchange. This was not the same policy as the November 2016 removal of specified notes’ legal-tender status.

Older Indian demonetisation episodes also cannot all be labelled Congress policy merely because they preceded 2014. This check has not reconstructed those earlier return percentages on a comparable basis.
history.comparison: Do not compare the 2016 return rate with routine replacement of still-valid designs as if the interventions were identical. A high return rate answers how much came back, not whether the policy met every stated objective.
sources: RBI, 3 March 2014 circular, old-series notes retain legal-tender status

title: How many people left poverty during UPA?
claim: UPA took 15 crore people out of poverty over its ten years in office.
summary: The official comparable series shows a 13.78-crore reduction from 2004–05 to 2011–12. It does not cover all ten years.
context: Indian Express reported the 15-crore statement from Gandhi’s 5 April 2014 Kasargode campaign speech.
evidence: The Planning Commission’s July 2013 Tendulkar estimates count 407.1 million poor people in 2004–05 and 269.3 million in 2011–12. The difference is 137.8 million, or 13.78 crore. The poverty ratio fell from 37.2% to 21.9%.
finding: Unverified for the exact 15-crore, ten-year claim. The official evidence supports a substantial decline during the available UPA-period window, but its end date is 2011–12, not 2014.
limit: A decline in estimated headcount is not a longitudinal count of identified individuals whose escape from poverty was caused solely by government policy. Monetary and multidimensional poverty measures must not be combined.
sources: Planning Commission, Tendulkar poverty estimates, 23 July 2013

before_2014: The same Tendulkar table gives a 45.3% poverty ratio in 1993–94, 37.2% in 2004–05 and 21.9% in 2011–12. The first interval spans several governments, including the NDA, rather than a single Congress administration.

The official estimated pace of decline was faster in 2004–05 to 2011–12. This is a survey-based consumption-poverty result, not proof that poverty disappeared or that all of the change came from a single programme.
history.comparison: Compare later governments with a compatible monetary-poverty method and survey design. A newer multidimensional index measures a different set of deprivations and is not a direct continuation of these headcounts.
sources: Planning Commission, Tendulkar poverty estimates, 23 July 2013

title: The 2013 land law: what UPA changed
claim: UPA brought in the new land-acquisition legislation to strengthen farmers’ protections.
summary: The replacement law was enacted in 2013 and took effect in January 2014. Its protections depended on acquisition category and procedure.
context: NDTV’s highlights of Gandhi’s 17 September 2013 Baran rally record him crediting UPA with the land-acquisition bill. The verdict checks the legislation, not his description of opponents’ intentions.
evidence: The 2013 Act replaced the 1894 law. It introduced a framework for social-impact assessment, compensation, rehabilitation and resettlement. For relevant acquisitions, the original law required consent of 70% of affected families for PPP projects and 80% for private-company projects.
finding: Supported for the enactment of the stronger statutory framework during UPA. It did not require the same consent threshold for every government acquisition or guarantee a fourfold payment in every rural case.
limit: This does not assess a particular land award or current state amendments. The value of the protection in practice depends on application, exemptions and enforcement.
sources: Rural Development Ministry, 2013 Act effective from 1 January 2014
PRS, 2013 law and proposed 2015 changes, consent and compensation

before_2014: The 1894 acquisition law remained the principal framework through earlier Congress and other governments until UPA’s replacement. Thus the reform has both a Congress-led enactment and a long earlier period in which governments, including Congress, used the old law.

The 2013 law took effect on 1 January 2014, before the change of Union government. Compensation combined statutory valuation, a rural multiplier where applicable and solatium. The shorthand “four times rural, twice urban” describes the broad framework, not every final award.
history.comparison: Compare the original 2013 protections with specific proposed or enacted later changes, rather than treating all land acquisition as one unchanging practice. A bill, an ordinance and a permanent enacted amendment are different legal stages.
sources: PRS, 2013 law and proposed 2015 changes, consent and compensation
Rural Development Ministry, 2013 Act effective from 1 January 2014

title: Did UPA establish a legal rural-employment guarantee?
claim: Congress-led UPA brought in the statutory rural-employment guarantee through MGNREGA.
summary: Yes. The household entitlement is distinct from a claim that everyone actually received 100 days of work.
context: PTI’s 27 July 2013 report records Gandhi listing the right to employment among UPA’s measures.
evidence: The CAG’s 2013 audit describes the legal guarantee for rural households whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work. Initial implementation began in 200 districts in February 2006 and expanded to all rural districts by April 2008.
finding: Supported for establishment of this statutory framework during UPA. It is not a guarantee of a permanent job or 100 days for each individual separately.
limit: This does not certify that every valid demand was met, every wage arrived on time, or the scheme was free of leakage. Later amendments and present-day delivery are outside this historical verdict.
sources: CAG, 2013 MGNREGA audit, programme history and delivery findings

before_2014: The programme’s UPA-era rollout created a substantial new legal framework. But the CAG found average employment per participating rural household fell from 54 days in 2009–10 to 43 in 2011–12, well below the 100-day headline. These averages alone do not show that every shortfall represented refused demand.
The audit covered implementation from April 2007 to March 2012 in sampled gram panchayats. It is evidence that implementation problems existed under UPA, not proof that nothing useful was delivered.
history.comparison: For comparisons with later governments, distinguish statutory entitlement, work demanded, work supplied, completed days and wage-payment delay. A larger nominal allocation alone does not establish better delivery.
sources: CAG, 2013 MGNREGA audit, programme history and delivery findings

title: RTI under UPA, with its earlier roots
claim: Congress-led UPA enacted the Right to Information Act.
summary: The 2005 law was enacted under UPA. The movement and earlier legislation were not confined to one government.
context: PTI reported Gandhi citing the right to information as a UPA measure in July 2013.
evidence: Official accounts identify the RTI Act as a 2005 enactment and its predecessor as the Freedom of Information Act, 2002. Section 31 of the RTI law repeals that predecessor.
finding: Supported for the enactment of the 2005 law during UPA. This is narrower than claiming Congress alone originated the right or that it always applied the transparency principle consistently.
limit: The verdict does not measure compliance, exemptions, appeal delays or every later amendment. The India Code PDF timed out during full retrieval; its indexed repeal clause is corroborated by the official historical account.
sources: Vice President’s official speech, 2002 and 2005 RTI enactments, 6 December 2017
India Code, RTI Act 2005, including section 31 repeal of 2002 predecessor

before_2014: The 2002 predecessor belongs to the earlier NDA period, while the 2005 law belongs to UPA-I. The distinction matters when assigning credit for legislation rather than claiming the underlying idea began with one party.

UPA’s own transparency record also had limits. In August 2013 its Cabinet approved introducing a bill to exclude political parties from the public-authority definition after the CIC had brought six parties, including Congress and BJP, within that definition. This was a proposal, not proof that the proposed exclusion became law.
history.comparison: Credit the enactment while also checking conduct under it. A party’s claim to have brought RTI does not settle its compliance with requests or its position on disclosure of its own affairs.
sources: Cabinet, proposal to exclude political parties from RTI, 2 August 2013

title: Right to Education: the 2002 foundation and 2009 law
claim: Congress-led UPA brought the Right to Education law into operation.
summary: The 2009 implementing law took effect in April 2010. Its constitutional foundation was enacted earlier under NDA.
context: Gandhi listed the right to education among UPA’s measures in the July 2013 statement reported by PTI.
evidence: The Education Ministry’s 2010 review dates enforcement of the RTE Act, 2009 to 1 April 2010 and expressly describes it as the consequential legislation to the 86th Constitutional Amendment of 2002.
finding: Supported for UPA’s implementing law and commencement. Exclusive credit for the constitutional foundation would omit the earlier amendment.
limit: The historical enactment is not proof that every child attended school, received good instruction or obtained any chosen private-school place. No nationwide implementation audit is made here.
sources: Education Ministry, RTE enactment and 86th Amendment chronology, 31 December 2010

before_2014: The 86th Amendment of 2002 established the Article 21A framework under the preceding NDA government. UPA’s 2009 legislation supplied the later statutory machinery and became operative in 2010. Both steps belong in the chronology.

The law addressed elementary education, with norms for schools and implementation through Union and state responsibilities. It should not be read as a universal free-college law or an assessment of all learning outcomes.
history.comparison: Separate the constitutional commitment, the implementing statute and actual classroom delivery. These are successive questions, rather than competing descriptions of one event.
sources: Education Ministry, RTE enactment and 86th Amendment chronology, 31 December 2010

title: Food security: a legal entitlement, with defined coverage
claim: UPA’s food-security measure created a legal entitlement to food support.
summary: The 2013 law created specified entitlements. It was not proof that hunger ended or that every adult received an unrestricted ration.
context: PTI’s July 2013 report records Gandhi presenting the food-security measure as a legal right. At that point an ordinance preceded completion of the parliamentary Act.
evidence: The December 2013 ministry review records notification of the NFSA on 10 September. It provides foodgrain coverage up to 75% of rural and 50% of urban population, specified household quantities, nutritional provisions, grievance redress and an allowance for non-supply.
finding: Supported for creating the legal framework under UPA. The scope and phased implementation matter when interpreting broad campaign claims about ending hunger.
limit: This is not a nutritional-outcome study or a current assessment of ration coverage. Entitlement and actual access must not be treated as identical.
sources: Food Ministry, NFSA coverage, entitlements and initial rollout, 20 December 2013

before_2014: NFSA built on the existing targeted public-distribution system and retained the Antyodaya category, rather than creating food distribution from nothing. The 2013 review gave priority-household grain at 5 kg per person per month and Antyodaya grain at 35 kg per household.

Implementation was gradual: the same December 2013 review named four states where it had begun. By February 2015, a later ministry reply listed eleven states/UTs receiving allocations under the Act. This distinguishes UPA-era enactment from subsequent rollout.
history.comparison: Credit the law’s creation and later governments’ implementation separately. New branding or a changed consumer price does not by itself erase the underlying 2013 entitlement. Delivery and nutritional outcomes need their own evidence.
sources: Food Ministry, eleven-state NFSA rollout as at February 2015
